addressed_problems.content: The paper's formal analysis linking sparsity to reduced out-of-distribution (OOD) detection risk is derived in a linear Gaussian toy model using the LASSO solution, which demonstrates that increasing sparsity reduces the influence of common features and improves the trade-off between ID classification and OOD rejection. However, the paper explicitly states that LASSO is not suitable for neural networks and that pruning is used heuristically, motivated by the linear analysis. Extending a rigorous theoretical justification of why and when pruning reduces OOD risk for nonlinear deep networks—identifying the conditions under which sparsity eliminates redundant features and mitigates overfitting in OOD detection—remains an unresolved open problem.

The primary pruning method used in the paper is iterative magnitude pruning with weight rewinding (Lottery Ticket Hypothesis, LTH), which is computationally intensive due to multiple training and pruning cycles. Although several during-training pruning methods (GMP, RigL, GraNet) were evaluated and shown to improve OOD detection, they yielded weaker OOD gains than LTH in these experiments. Designing more efficient pruning schedules or training-time sparse training algorithms that match or exceed LTH's OOD benefits without the computational overhead of iterative pruning remains an unresolved practical and algorithmic challenge.

Model averaging is empirically shown to stabilize OOD detection metrics (AUROC, FPR95) by smoothing the loss landscape and approximating the behavior of ensembles, yet a formal understanding of how parameter averaging affects OOD scoring functions is lacking. The paper provides only empirical landscape visualizations to demonstrate stability under weight perturbations, but does not offer theoretical guarantees connecting averaging to the robustness of OOD metrics. A formal characterization of the relationship between weight averaging and the stability of threshold-independent OOD detection scores remains an unresolved theoretical issue.

The hyperparameters for pruning (pruning fraction per iteration, rewind step k, number of pruning iterations) and model averaging (starting epoch t0, decay rate τ) are set empirically based on CIFAR benchmarks (e.g., 20% pruning per iteration, 9 iterations, t0=100). The paper does not provide a principled selection method or theoretical guidelines for transferring these hyperparameters across different architectures, dataset scales, or varying OOD difficulty regimes (near-OOD vs far-OOD). Determining how to choose these hyperparameters in a principled and transferable manner remains an open practical question.

Deep classifiers deployed in open-world settings must distinguish in-distribution (ID) inputs (drawn from the classes seen at training time) from out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs (semantic inputs not belonging to those classes). Prior work has focused largely on designing post-hoc scoring functions (e.g. MSP, ODIN, Mahalanobis, energy score, ViM) or on using auxiliary outlier datasets (Outlier Exposure) and on improved architectures (e.g. transformers) to obtain better OOD discrimination. These prior approaches tacitly assume that the final trained checkpoint is a reliable basis for OOD scoring and do not analyze the behavior of OOD metrics during training. As a result, two substantive gaps remain prior to this work: (1) the training-dynamics gap — how OOD detection performance (e.g. AUROC, FPR95) evolves along the optimizer trajectory is not characterized, so practitioners must pick a final checkpoint without guidance despite potentially large metric swings; and (2) the overparameterization / memorization gap — modern overparameterized networks can continue training after near-zero training error and thereby memorize training idiosyncrasies and learn abundant, weak "common" features shared between ID and OOD data; this learning increases overlap between ID and OOD feature distributions and degrades OOD detection. Concretely, because prior methods (scoring functions, ensembling, or use of auxiliary outliers) operate at evaluation-time and do not control the emergence of redundant or noisy features during continued training, they cannot (a) prevent AUROC from decreasing as training proceeds toward zero training error, (b) prevent sharp checkpoint-to-checkpoint instability of AUROC near the end of training, or (c) provide a principled, model-level mechanism to suppress learning of abundant non-discriminative common features that increase OOD risk. These unresolved issues cause practical consequences: unreliable model selection (a nearby checkpoint may have much worse OOD performance), systematic deterioration of OOD metrics despite improving classification loss, and lack of a simple, architecture-agnostic training-time module to stabilize and improve OOD detection.

nodes.content: In standard image-classification training, practitioners monitor classification loss/accuracy but not OOD metrics along optimization. The community had not characterized whether OOD metrics track classification metrics or exhibit distinct behavior. Without such a characterization, there is no empirical basis to (i) decide when to stop training for best OOD detection; (ii) understand whether late-stage training harms OOD performance; nor (iii) diagnose whether checkpoint instability (large metric changes for small weight perturbations or small training-time advances) is present. This absence of visibility prevents principled mitigation: one cannot tell whether degradation in AUROC is due to model capacity, optimization noise, or learned redundant features, so prior post-hoc scoring or ensembling approaches cannot address the root cause. The three-stage description provides the missing empirical baseline needed to motivate interventions targeted at the late-stage overfitting and instability.

Practitioners observe that AUROC may vary sharply between nearby checkpoints, but without a mechanistic account of the instability they cannot choose a robust final model. Prior remedies (post-hoc rescoring, temperature scaling, or ensembling) either operate at evaluation time or incur large computational cost (ensembling requires training multiple models). The instability diagnosis requires identifying a source tied to geometry of the loss/score landscape: if the OOD scoring function sits on a narrow valley, small weight changes (due to SGD noise or checkpointing) can flip OOD decisions. Averaging parameters along the trajectory is a low-cost way to approximate ensemble behavior and to bias optimization toward wider minima; but whether such averaging actually reduces AUROC instability was not established. This conclusion resolves that question by showing a concrete averaging rule that stabilizes OOD metrics, providing a practical, low-overhead remedy aligned with the empirical instability mechanism.

Empirical evidence hinted that overparameterized networks learn many weak, noisy features that exist across datasets and thereby increase the overlap between ID and OOD feature distributions, but a precise analytic connection was missing. Without an explicit model demonstrating how abundance of weak common features ($d$) affects classification vs. rejection trade-offs, there is no principled motivation for employing sparsity-inducing regularizers or pruning as a remedy. The linear-Gaussian derivation and the closed-form LASSO solution provide a transparent setting linking $d,\eta,\sigma,\lambda$ to ID and OOD risks, thereby justifying a sparsity-based intervention and giving guidance (e.g. $\lambda\approx\eta$) for selecting regularization strength in the toy regime. This resolves the conceptual gap that previously prevented theory-grounded pruning for OOD detection.

There was no simple, reproducible, training-time module that simultaneously addresses the two distinct failure modes identified (late-stage overfitting that increases ID/OOD overlap; and checkpoint instability of OOD metrics). Prior ensemble-based stability remedies require training multiple full models (expensive), and LASSO-style feature selection cannot be directly applied to deep networks. Iterative magnitude pruning with rewind (LTH / IMP) is an established post-training mechanism for yielding sparse subnetworks, and moving-weight averaging is an established low-cost technique for widening minima; however, neither was previously combined and evaluated as a unified, pluggable pipeline for OOD detection. AoP fills that operational gap by specifying concrete pruning fractions, rewind protocol, and averaging schedule that can be applied on top of existing OOD scoring procedures, enabling practitioners to mitigate both instability and overfitting without redesigning scoring functions.

Benchmarks prior to this work reported many isolated OOD improvements tied to particular scoring functions or auxiliary-data training, but it was unclear whether a unified, training-time module could yield consistent gains across scoring functions, architectures, and dataset scales. Practitioners lacked a simple "plug-in" to systematically improve OOD metrics while preserving classification accuracy. The empirical claim that AoP produces substantial, consistent improvements resolves that applied gap by demonstrating transferable gains (quantified in AUROC / FPR95 percentages) across the common CIFAR and ImageNet benchmarks and across scoring methods.

Although pruning is a mainstream compression technique, its impact on OOD detection was not characterized: does pruning help by removing common noisy features, or does reducing capacity always harm OOD detection? Practitioners need to know whether compressing models is acceptable or beneficial for safety-critical OOD tasks and which pruning algorithms are suitable. The reported non-monotone relation between sparsity and AUROC and the empirical superiority of LTH with rewind provide the missing evidence: moderate sparsity improves OOD detection by pruning common features, but overly aggressive pruning removes useful signals, and pruning algorithm/initialization choices materially affect OOD outcomes.

It was unclear whether the two proposed remedies address a single root cause or complementary failure modes: if pruning alone sufficed, then averaging would be unnecessary; conversely, if averaging alone sufficed, pruning would be superfluous. Without ablation, practitioners could not prioritize interventions given limited computational budgets. Demonstrating that both pruning and averaging jointly yield larger gains resolves this method-selection ambiguity and justifies the two-part AoP design.

OOD detection and misclassification detection both measure whether a model "knows what it does not know", but methods that improve one may not improve the other. Prior work frequently treats the two tasks separately. Practitioners deploying models in safety-critical settings need unified techniques that improve both types of uncertainty-awareness. The observed AoP gains on misclassification detection indicate the approach addresses a common underlying weakness (overconfident decisions induced by redundant, noisy features and narrow minima), thereby resolving the practical question of cross-task benefit.

The trajectory of out-of-distribution (OOD) detection performance, measured by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and related metrics, during supervised training decomposes into three distinct stages: (A) an initial stage where training and test error fall and AUROC improves; (B) a subsequent overfitting stage where the training error approaches zero and test error can continue to decrease while AUROC decreases (i.e., OOD performance degrades as the model memorizes and learns redundant features); and (C) a final instability stage where classification test error is stable but AUROC (and other OOD metrics) varies sharply across nearby checkpoints, making final-checkpoint selection unreliable.

metadata.narrative: The three-stage characterization (C1) is supported by strong cross-dataset (H1), cross-metric (H2), and cross-architecture (H3) evidence, which collectively underwrite the generalization of the pattern across OOD datasets, metrics, and architectures. However, P1 identifies a load-bearing risk: the observed pattern may be specific to the step-decay learning rate schedule used in the experiments, as the stage transitions align with LR drops. This risk primarily affects the generalization layer of the conclusion: the pattern is reliably established for the tested schedule but its universality across training schedules remains unverified. The highlights do not directly offset P1 because they all use the same schedule, so the residual risk on the generalization layer is meaningful.

nodes.title: Empirical characterization: three-stage training dynamics of out-of-distribution metrics

nodes.content:
The instability of out-of-distribution (OOD) metrics near the final checkpoint arises from the trained solution being fragile to small perturbations of network weights: evaluating the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and the false positive rate at 95% true positive rate (FPR95) as the weights are moved along random normalized directions \(d\) with small scalar magnitude \(\alpha\) (i.e., \(\theta(d,\alpha)=\theta_{\text{final}}+\alpha\cdot d\)) shows narrow optima in the weight space causing sharp metric changes for small \(\alpha\). Applying exponential moving-weight averaging (Model Averaging, MA) stabilizes OOD performance by producing a smoother / wider optimum: MA is implemented as the exponential moving average of parameters after an epoch \(t_0\),
      \[
      \theta_{t+1}^{\mathrm{MA}}=\begin{cases}
      \theta_t, & t<t_0,\\[4pt]
      \tau\cdot \theta_t^{\mathrm{MA}} + (1-\tau)\cdot \theta_{t+1}, & t\ge t_0,
      \end{cases}
      \]
      with \(\tau=\dfrac{t-t_0}{t-t_0+1}\). The averaged parameters \(\theta^{\mathrm{MA}}\) yield substantially reduced AUROC and FPR95 sensitivity to small weight perturbations and smoother AUROC curves during training across scoring functions.

metadata.narrative: The instability diagnosis and MA remedy (C2) are strongly supported by direct landscape visualization (H4) showing narrow optima in AUROC/FPR95 under weight perturbations, and by cross-scoring-function stabilization evidence (H5). P2 raises a concern that the random-direction perturbation may not represent actual SGD noise, which would weaken the mechanistic link between narrow optima and checkpoint instability. However, H4's quantitative demonstration that small perturbations cause large metric changes is direct evidence of fragility, and H5 shows that MA empirically stabilizes metrics regardless of the exact perturbation direction. The residual risk from P2 is partially offset by the empirical robustness of the MA remedy, which does not depend on the exact cause of instability. The conclusion's practical recommendation (use MA) is well-supported even if the mechanistic diagnosis is imperfect.

nodes.title: Instability source and remedy: model fragility under small weight perturbations; model averaging stabilizes out-of-distribution metrics

nodes.content:
For a simplified linear-Gaussian model that isolates a special discriminative feature and \(d\) abundant weak common features, the Bayes classifier and its in-distribution (ID) classification risk and out-of-distribution (OOD) detection (rejection) risk admit closed-form expressions: let ID feature vectors \(\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1}\) be drawn as \(\boldsymbol{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(y \cdot \boldsymbol{\mu}_\text{ID}, \sigma^2 \boldsymbol{I})\) with \(y\stackrel{u.a.r.}{\sim}\{-1,+1\}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_\text{ID}=(1,\eta,\dots,\eta)\), and OOD feature vectors be drawn as \(\boldsymbol{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(q \cdot \boldsymbol{\mu}_\text{OOD}, \sigma^2 \boldsymbol{I})\) with \(q\stackrel{u.a.r.}{\sim}\{-1,+1\}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_\text{OOD}=(0,\eta,\dots,\eta)\), with isotropic noise variance \(\sigma^2\). The Bayes logit is
      \[
      f_{\mathrm{Bayes}}(\boldsymbol{x}) = x_1 + \eta\sum_{i=2}^{d+1} x_i,
      \]
      and the resulting risks simplify to
      \[
      \mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{ID}}(f_{\mathrm{Bayes}})=\Pr\!\left\{\mathcal{N}(0,1)>\frac{\sqrt{1+d\eta^2}}{\sigma}\right\},
      \]
      \[
      \mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{OOD}}(f_{\mathrm{Bayes}})=\Pr\!\left\{\mathcal{N}(0,1)>\frac{\delta-d\eta^2}{\sigma\sqrt{1+d\eta^2}}\right\}+\Pr\!\left\{\mathcal{N}(0,1)>\frac{\delta+d\eta^2}{\sigma\sqrt{1+d\eta^2}}\right\},
      \]
      where \(\delta\) is the rejection threshold. These formulas show that increasing the number \(d\) of common weak features (with \(0<\eta\ll1\) and \(d\gg1\)) can markedly increase OOD risk while only slowly improving ID classification. Further, solving the squared-error empirical risk with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regularization parameter \(\lambda\),
      \[
      \min_{\boldsymbol{w}}\ \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_\text{ID}}\!\left\{\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\boldsymbol{w}^\top\boldsymbol{x}}{\sigma}-y\right)^2+\lambda\|\boldsymbol{w}\|_1\right\},
      \]
      yields the closed-form trimmed coefficient vector
      \[
      f_{\text{LASSO}}(\boldsymbol{x}) = (1-\lambda)_+\,x_1 + \sum_{i=2}^{d+1} (\eta-\lambda)_+\, x_i,
      \]
      where \((\cdot)_+\) denotes the positive part. This analytic solution demonstrates that an \(L_1\) penalty (feature selection) can suppress coefficients on abundant weak common features (by choosing \(\lambda\approx\eta\)), thereby reducing OOD detection risk at controlled cost to ID accuracy.

metadata.narrative: The theoretical analysis (C3) is rigorously derived (H6, H7) within the linear-Gaussian model, providing closed-form expressions that clearly link common features to OOD risk and show how LASSO suppresses them. P3 identifies the fundamental limitation: the model is a drastic simplification of deep neural network feature learning, so the quantitative formulas do not directly apply to the empirical setting. This risk is not offset by any highlight, as the paper acknowledges that LASSO is not suitable for neural networks and uses pruning heuristically. The conclusion's value lies in providing intuition and motivation for pruning, but the theoretical justification for the specific pruning mechanism in deep networks remains heuristic. The qualitative direction (sparsity helps OOD) is supported by the theory, but the quantitative predictions are not transferable.

nodes.title: Linear-Gaussian risk formulas and LASSO solution: analytic link between common features, in-distribution accuracy and out-of-distribution risk

nodes.content:
Average of Pruning (AoP) is a practical, architecture-agnostic pipeline combining iterative magnitude pruning with parameter averaging to mitigate overfitting and instability for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection. Operationally, AoP comprises three steps: (1) apply iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) with weight-rewinding (the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis with rewind protocol): initialize mask \(m = 1^n\) (all weights retained), train from \(\theta_0\) to \(\theta_k\), then iteratively train \(m \odot \theta_k\) to \(m \odot \theta_T\), prune the lowest-magnitude 20% of weights globally to update \(m\), and rewind weights to \(\theta_k\), repeating for a number of iterations \(N\) (with 20% pruning per iteration and 9 iterations reaching approximately 86% sparsity in CIFAR experiments); (2) during or after pruning, compute an exponential moving average of parameters per
      \[
      \theta_{t+1}^{\mathrm{MA}}=\begin{cases}
      \theta_t, & t<t_0,\\[4pt]
      \tau\cdot \theta_t^{\mathrm{MA}} + (1-\tau)\cdot \theta_{t+1}, & t\ge t_0,
      \end{cases}
      \]
      with \(t_0=100\) epochs for CIFAR training and \(\tau = (t-t_0)/(t-t_0+1)\); (3) use the averaged, pruned model \(f(x; m\odot \theta^{\mathrm{MA}})\) as a drop-in replacement for any post-hoc OOD scoring method (e.g., Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP), Out-of-DIstribution detector for Neural networks (ODIN), energy-based scoring (Energy), Virtual-Logit Matching (ViM), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)). AoP is designed to be low-barrier: pruning reduces learned common features (addressing overfitting), and model averaging widens optima (addressing instability); the combined module is applied without modifying existing scoring functions.

metadata.narrative: The AoP algorithm (C4) is clearly specified (H8) and shown to be compatible with multiple scoring functions and OE (H9), supporting its claim as a pluggable module. P4 identifies a load-bearing risk: the hyperparameters (pruning fraction, iterations, rewind step, MA start epoch) are empirically chosen and their sensitivity is not analyzed. This risk affects the practical utility layer: users may need to re-tune for new settings. H8 and H9 do not offset this risk because they address reproducibility and compatibility, not hyperparameter robustness. The conclusion that AoP is a "simple module readily pluggable" is somewhat overstated given the tuning required, but the method's core idea is sound.

nodes.title: Algorithmic contribution: Average of Pruning (AoP) — combine iterative magnitude pruning with model averaging as a pluggable out-of-distribution module

nodes.content: Applying Average of Pruning (AoP) as a plug-in improves out-of-distribution (OOD) detection performance across multiple benchmarks and scoring methods. Representative results: on ResNet-18 trained on CIFAR-10, applying AoP to K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) increases average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) across six OOD datasets from 94.39% to 95.04% and reduces average false positive rate at 95% true positive rate (FPR95) from 34.42% to 25.30% (a 9.1 percentage-point decrease); applying AoP to Virtual-Logit Matching (ViM) on the same backbone/dataset increases average AUROC from 94.18% to 95.69% and reduces FPR95 from 32.27% to 25.3%. AoP also improves multiple scoring functions (e.g., Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP), MaxLogit) and scales to larger datasets: on Tiny-ImageNet, AoP improves MSP AUROC by 1.5–3.3 percentage points on Textures, LSUN, and iSUN; on ImageNet, AoP yields AUROC improvements of 0.3–0.7 percentage points across scoring functions on Places, SUN, and Textures. The improvements hold across backbones (ResNet variants, WideResNet, VGG, MobileNet) and remain when combining AoP with Outlier Exposure (OE).

metadata.narrative: The empirical efficacy of AoP (C5) is supported by comprehensive evaluation across datasets, architectures, and scoring functions (H10), with large FPR95 reductions on CIFAR benchmarks (H11) that demonstrate practical significance. P5 identifies a statistical risk: the lack of significance tests and small improvements on ImageNet mean that some reported gains might not be statistically reliable. H10 and H11 partially offset this risk by showing that the large CIFAR improvements are well outside the noise range, but the ImageNet results remain vulnerable. The conclusion is well-supported for CIFAR-scale experiments, with weaker support for ImageNet-scale.

nodes.title: Empirical efficacy: Average of Pruning consistently improves out-of-distribution detection metrics across datasets, scoring functions and architectures

nodes.content: Iterative magnitude pruning (Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) style with weight rewinding) reduces the late-stage overfitting of out-of-distribution (OOD) detection: as global sparsity is increased from dense toward moderate sparsity, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) on OOD tasks first increases (pruning removes redundant common features that induce in-distribution (ID) / OOD overlap) and then eventually decreases if pruning becomes too aggressive and removes discriminative capacity. Visualization of final-layer features shows pruned models produce larger ID-versus-OOD feature differences than dense models. Different pruning schedules and methods matter: LTH with weight rewind outperforms random pruning and naive fine-tuning based pruning in OOD metrics, and among during-training pruning methods evaluated (Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP), Rigging the Lottery (RigL), Gradual Network with neuroregeneration (GraNet)), iterative/post-training LTH performed best for OOD tasks in CIFAR-10 experiments with ResNet-18.

metadata.narrative: The pruning analysis (C6) is supported by systematic sparsity sweeps (H12) showing the non-monotone relationship across datasets and architectures, and by comparisons across pruning methods (H13) showing that LTH with rewind is most effective. P6 identifies a risk in the feature separation visualization: the qualitative single-batch evidence does not quantitatively establish that pruning increases ID/OOD feature separation. H12 and H13 do not directly offset this risk because they focus on AUROC improvements rather than feature analysis. The conclusion that pruning reduces OOD overfitting is well-supported by the AUROC evidence, but the mechanistic claim about feature separation is less solid.

nodes.title: Pruning reduces out-of-distribution overfitting and produces feature separation; non-monotone sparsity dependence

nodes.content: Ablation experiments establish that both components—model averaging (MA) and pruning—are required: (i) pruning alone improves the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) relative to the dense baseline, and (ii) combining pruning with MA (Average of Pruning, AoP) yields the best performance. For example on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18: baseline AUROC = 91.63%; with pruning alone AUROC increases to 92.94%; with pruning plus MA (AoP) AUROC further increases to 93.32%. Similar trends hold for WideResNet-28-10 and other metrics (area under the precision-recall curve (AUPR), false positive rate at 95% true positive rate (FPR95)), showing complementary roles: pruning reduces overfitting and MA stabilizes the weights/landscape for more reliable scoring.

metadata.narrative: The ablation study (C7) provides clear comparative evidence (H14) that both pruning and MA contribute to the full AoP gain on the tested setting (MSP on CIFAR-10). P7 identifies a generalization risk: the ablation is limited to one scoring function and one dataset, and does not include an "MA only" condition to fully isolate each component's contribution. H14 does not offset this risk because it uses the same limited setting. The conclusion that both components are necessary is supported for MSP on CIFAR-10, but its generality across scoring functions and datasets is not established.

nodes.title: Ablation: both model averaging and pruning are necessary to realize full Average of Pruning gains

nodes.content: Average of Pruning (AoP) not only improves out-of-distribution (OOD) detection but also enhances misclassification detection (detecting when the classifier will be wrong on in-distribution inputs). On WideResNet-40-2 trained on CIFAR-10, applying AoP to Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP) improves the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) for misclassification detection from 92.51% to 93.23%, reduces the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC) from \(7.55\times 10^{-3}\) to \(6.41\times 10^{-3}\), and reduces the false positive rate at 95% true positive rate (FPR95) from 40.87% to 38.47%. Similar improvements are observed when AoP is combined with other confidence estimators (e.g., Confidence-aware Learning (CRL)).

metadata.narrative: The misclassification detection results (C8) show consistent improvements across multiple architectures and metrics (H15), supporting the claim that AoP benefits this related task. P8 identifies risks of limited scope (only CIFAR-10/100) and small effect sizes without significance testing. H15 partially offsets the scope concern by showing consistency across architectures, but the small improvements and lack of large-scale validation leave the practical significance uncertain. The conclusion is supported for small-scale settings but its generalization to larger datasets is not demonstrated.

nodes.title: Average of Pruning improves misclassification (error) detection as well as out-of-distribution detection

nodes.content: The three-stage pattern of the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) during training—initial improvement, overfitting decline, and final instability—observed for a ResNet-18 trained on CIFAR-10 with a step-decay learning rate schedule (initial learning rate 0.1, decay by factor 0.1 at epochs 100 and 150) is not established for other learning rate schedules (e.g., cosine annealing, constant learning rate) because the stage transitions align with the learning rate drops and no experiments with alternative schedules are provided.

metadata.failure_mode: If the three-stage pattern is an artifact of the step-decay schedule, then the conclusion that OOD detection dynamics decompose into three distinct stages during supervised training would be valid only for this specific schedule, not for supervised training in general. The practical implication that practitioners should monitor OOD metrics and avoid late-stage checkpoints would be schedule-dependent, potentially misleading for those using other schedules where OOD metrics might behave differently (e.g., monotonic improvement or stable plateau).
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper only evaluates one training schedule (step decay at epochs 100 and 150) for the three-stage characterization. The transitions between stages align with the LR decay points: stage A ends around epoch 100 when LR first drops, stage B spans epochs 100-150, and stage C starts after epoch 150 when LR drops again. This temporal alignment raises the possibility that the observed dynamics are driven by the schedule rather than an inherent property of OOD detection. Without experiments using alternative schedules (cosine annealing, constant LR, or no decay), the claim that the three-stage pattern is a general property of supervised training for OOD detection is not established.

nodes.title: Learning rate schedule dependence of three-stage pattern

nodes.content: For a ResNet-18 trained on CIFAR-10, the analysis of the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and false positive rate at 95% true positive rate (FPR95) sensitivity to weight perturbations uses random Gaussian directions d normalized as in prior work and evaluates the landscape along \(\theta_{\text{final}} + \alpha \cdot d\) for scalar \(\alpha\). The claim that the trained solution is fragile to small weight perturbations (narrow optima) is based on these random directions, which may not represent the actual directions of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) weight updates during training; the model could be robust to perturbations along the training trajectory while being fragile to arbitrary random directions.

metadata.failure_mode: If the narrow optima are an artifact of random-direction probing and do not reflect actual SGD behavior, then the mechanistic explanation for checkpoint instability (fragility to small weight perturbations) would be unsupported. The conclusion that model averaging stabilizes OOD metrics by widening optima would still be empirically valid (since MA empirically improves stability), but the causal link to the landscape geometry would be weakened. The practical recommendation to use MA would remain, but the theoretical grounding would be less solid.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper does not justify that random Gaussian directions are representative of the weight changes that occur during SGD training. The weight updates in SGD are structured (gradient-based, with momentum and weight decay), whereas random directions explore all dimensions equally. The model might have learned features that are robust to perturbations along the training trajectory but not to arbitrary random directions. Without comparing the AUROC sensitivity along the actual training trajectory (e.g., between consecutive checkpoints) to that along random directions, the claim that instability arises from narrow optima in weight space is not directly supported.

nodes.title: Random direction perturbation not representative of stochastic gradient descent noise

nodes.content: In a linear-Gaussian model where in-distribution (ID) features are drawn from \(\mathcal{N}(y \cdot \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{ID}}, \sigma^2 \boldsymbol{I})\) with \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{ID}} = (1, \eta, \dots, \eta) \in \mathbb{R}^{d+1}\) and out-of-distribution (OOD) features from \(\mathcal{N}(q \cdot \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{OOD}}, \sigma^2 \boldsymbol{I})\) with \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{OOD}} = (0, \eta, \dots, \eta)\), and where the first feature is discriminative (special) while the remaining \(d\) features are common (same mean \(\eta\) for both ID and OOD), the derived Bayes optimal classifier and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) solution provide closed-form risk expressions. However, this model assumes independent features with identical common-feature strength \(\eta\) and isotropic noise, which is a drastic simplification of the feature representations learned by deep neural networks where features are correlated, have varying degrees of sharedness, and interact nonlinearly.

metadata.failure_mode: If the linear-Gaussian model is not representative of real neural network feature learning, then the theoretical justification for pruning (that it reduces common features and thus OOD risk) is weakened. The conclusion that pruning eliminates overfitting by removing redundant common features would still be empirically supported (by the experiments in C6), but the theoretical link from the LASSO analysis to the pruning mechanism would be heuristic rather than rigorous. The specific guidance that $\lambda \approx \eta$ (i.e., pruning should target features with small coefficients) would not be directly transferable.
metadata.weakness_reason: The model assumes that all common features have the same mean $\eta$ for both ID and OOD, that they are independent, and that noise is isotropic. In practice, features learned by neural networks are highly correlated, the degree of "commonness" varies across features, and interactions are nonlinear. The paper acknowledges that "LASSO is not suitable for neural networks" but does not discuss the limitations of the linear-Gaussian model itself. Without empirical validation that the qualitative behavior (increasing $d$ harms OOD more than ID) holds in real networks, the theoretical analysis provides intuition but not a rigorous foundation for the pruning intervention.

nodes.title: Linear-Gaussian model is a drastic simplification

nodes.content: The Average of Pruning (AoP) pipeline uses iterative magnitude pruning with weight rewind (20% pruning per iteration, 9 iterations reaching approximately 86% sparsity on CIFAR-10/100 experiments) and exponential moving average of parameters starting at epoch \(t_0 = 100\) with decay \(\tau = (t - t_0) / (t - t_0 + 1)\). These hyperparameters are empirically chosen for CIFAR-10/100 with step-decay schedule, and no sensitivity analysis or principled selection method is provided for new datasets, architectures, or training schedules, so the performance of AoP may depend on these specific choices.

metadata.failure_mode: If AoP's hyperparameters require careful tuning for each new dataset/architecture, then the conclusion that AoP is a "simple module readily pluggable into any existing method" would be overstated. The practical utility would be reduced because users would need to perform additional validation to select hyperparameters. The reported improvements on CIFAR and ImageNet might not transfer to other settings without similar tuning effort.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper does not analyze the sensitivity of AoP's performance to its hyperparameters (pruning fraction, number of iterations, rewind step, MA start epoch). The choices (20% per iteration, 9 iterations, $t_0 = 100$) are stated but not justified through ablation or sensitivity analysis. For ImageNet experiments, the paper uses one-shot pruning (80% sparsity) instead of iterative pruning, indicating that the protocol is not fixed. Without a sensitivity analysis, it is unclear whether the reported improvements are robust to reasonable variations in these hyperparameters or whether they require careful tuning for each new setting.

nodes.title: Average of Pruning hyperparameters are empirically chosen without sensitivity analysis

nodes.content: The reported improvements in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and false positive rate at 95% true positive rate (FPR95) for Average of Pruning (AoP) over baseline methods on CIFAR-10/100 (e.g., K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) AUROC from 94.39% to 95.04%, FPR95 from 34.42% to 25.30%) are accompanied by standard deviations over 5 runs, but no statistical significance tests (e.g., paired t-tests or confidence intervals for the differences) are provided. On ImageNet, no error bars or run information is reported, and some improvements are small (e.g., Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP) AUROC on Places from 76.26 to 76.58), making it unclear whether the improvements are statistically significant or within the noise of a single run.

metadata.failure_mode: If the improvements are not statistically significant, then the conclusion that AoP consistently improves OOD detection metrics would be unsupported for those cases where the gains are small. The practical recommendation to use AoP would be weakened, as users might not see reliable improvements. The overall narrative of AoP's effectiveness would be reduced to only those settings where gains are large and clearly significant (e.g., CIFAR-10 KNN FPR95 reduction of 9.1 points).
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper reports mean and standard deviation over 5 runs for CIFAR experiments, but does not perform any statistical test to compare AoP against baselines. For ImageNet experiments (Table 5), no error bars or run information is provided. Some improvements are very small (e.g., 0.32 AUROC points for MSP on Places) and could be within the noise of a single run. Without statistical testing, the claim that AoP "consistently improves" OOD detection is based on the direction of the mean differences rather than on evidence that the differences are unlikely to occur by chance.

nodes.title: Lack of statistical significance testing for Average of Pruning improvements

nodes.content: For a ResNet-18 trained on CIFAR-10, the claim that pruning increases the difference between in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) feature representations is supported by a single visualization showing the absolute difference of final-layer features for a dense model versus a sparse model on one random batch of CIFAR-10 (ID) and LSUN (OOD) data. No quantitative metrics (e.g., mean feature distance, cosine similarity, or distribution divergence across multiple batches) are provided to support this claim, so the visualization may not be representative of the overall feature distributions.

metadata.failure_mode: If the feature separation claim is not quantitatively supported, then the mechanistic explanation for why pruning improves OOD detection (by reducing common features and increasing ID/OOD feature differences) would be weakened. The conclusion that pruning reduces OOD overfitting would still be supported by the AUROC improvements, but the proposed mechanism (feature separation) would be less credible. The theoretical link between the linear-Gaussian model and the empirical pruning results would be less direct.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper states that "most of the features from ID or OOD dataset are similar for dense model. However, their difference are more obvious for sparse model" based on a single visualization. No quantitative metrics (e.g., mean feature distance, cosine similarity, or distribution divergence) are provided to support this claim. The visualization shows the absolute difference of features for one batch, which could be influenced by the specific samples chosen. Without statistical quantification across multiple batches or a formal measure of feature overlap, the claim that pruning increases feature separation is based on anecdotal visual evidence.

nodes.title: Feature separation visualization is qualitative and not quantified

nodes.content: The ablation study for Average of Pruning (AoP) evaluates three conditions—baseline (no model averaging (MA), no pruning), pruning only, and pruning plus MA—using the Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP) scoring function on CIFAR-10 for ResNet-18 and WideResNet-28-10. It does not test whether both components are necessary for other scoring functions (e.g., K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Virtual-Logit Matching (ViM), energy-based scoring) or other datasets (e.g., CIFAR-100, ImageNet), and it does not include an "MA only without pruning" condition to isolate the contribution of each component independently.

metadata.failure_mode: If the necessity of both components does not hold for other scoring functions or datasets, then the conclusion that "both model averaging and pruning are necessary to realize full AoP gains" would be overgeneralized. Practitioners using different scoring functions might find that pruning alone is sufficient, or that MA alone is sufficient, making the full AoP pipeline unnecessary. The design justification for AoP as a two-part method would be weakened.
metadata.weakness_reason: The ablation only covers one scoring function (MSP) and one dataset (CIFAR-10). The paper does not test whether pruning alone suffices for other scoring functions (e.g., KNN might benefit more from MA than from pruning) or whether MA alone might be sufficient for some settings. The absence of an "MA only" condition means the paper cannot distinguish between the case where both are necessary and the case where MA alone achieves the same improvement as the combination. The small additional gain from MA on top of pruning (0.38 AUROC points for ResNet-18) could be within noise.

nodes.title: Ablation study limited to one scoring function and one dataset

nodes.content: The evaluation of Average of Pruning (AoP) for misclassification detection is conducted on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 using WideResNet-40-2, VGG-16, and ResNet-18 with Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP) and Confidence-aware Learning (CRL) baselines. The improvements are small (e.g., area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) from 92.51% to 93.23% for MSP on WideResNet-40-2, from 93.41% to 93.77% for MSP on ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10) and no statistical significance tests are reported. The generalization to larger-scale datasets (e.g., ImageNet) or other architectures is not demonstrated.

metadata.failure_mode: If the improvements do not generalize to larger datasets or are not statistically significant, then the conclusion that AoP improves misclassification detection would be limited to the tested settings. The practical significance for safety-critical applications (which often involve large-scale models) would be unclear.
metadata.weakness_reason: The misclassification detection experiments are conducted only on CIFAR-10/100, which are relatively small-scale datasets. The improvements are modest (less than 1 AUROC point in most cases) and no error bars or significance tests are provided for the misclassification detection results (Table 8). The paper does not test on ImageNet or other large-scale datasets where misclassification detection might behave differently. Without broader evaluation, the claim that AoP improves misclassification detection is supported only for small-scale settings.

nodes.title: Misclassification detection evaluation limited to small-scale datasets

nodes.content: For a ResNet-18 trained on CIFAR-10 with step-decay learning rate schedule, the three-stage pattern of AUROC during training—initial improvement, overfitting decline, and final instability—is observed across six out-of-distribution datasets: Textures, SVHN, LSUN-Crop, LSUN-Resize, Place365, and iSUN, with each dataset showing qualitatively similar behavior of AUROC decreasing after near-zero training error and exhibiting sharp fluctuations in the final training stage.

metadata.credit: This cross-dataset consistency preempts the concern that the three-stage pattern might be specific to a particular OOD dataset (e.g., LSUN-Resize). Without this evidence, the conclusion would be vulnerable to the criticism that the observed dynamics are driven by dataset-specific artifacts. The credit underwrites the generalization of the three-stage characterization across OOD datasets, supporting the claim that the pattern is a general property of OOD detection dynamics during training.

nodes.title: Three-stage pattern observed across six OOD datasets

nodes.content: For a ResNet-18 trained on CIFAR-10 with step-decay learning rate schedule, the three-stage pattern is observed not only for AUROC but also for AUPR (area under precision-recall curve) and FPR95 (false positive rate at 95% true positive rate) when evaluated on LSUN-Resize as OOD data, with all three metrics showing a decline after near-zero training error and instability in the final stage.

metadata.credit: This multi-metric consistency preempts the concern that the three-stage pattern might be an artifact of the AUROC metric's sensitivity to threshold or class imbalance. Without this evidence, the conclusion would be vulnerable to the criticism that only AUROC shows this pattern while other metrics (e.g., FPR95) might behave differently. The credit underwrites the measurement validity of the three-stage characterization, showing it is not metric-specific.

nodes.title: Three-stage pattern observed across multiple metrics

nodes.content: For a WideResNet-28-10 trained on CIFAR-10 with step-decay learning rate schedule, the three-stage pattern of AUROC during training—initial improvement, overfitting decline, and final instability—is observed across six out-of-distribution datasets (Textures, SVHN, LSUN-Crop, LSUN-Resize, Place365, iSUN), indicating that the pattern is not specific to the ResNet-18 architecture.

metadata.credit: This cross-architecture consistency preempts the concern that the three-stage pattern might be specific to the ResNet-18 architecture (e.g., due to its particular depth or width). Without this evidence, the conclusion would be vulnerable to the criticism that the dynamics are architecture-dependent. The credit underwrites the generalization of the three-stage characterization across network architectures.

nodes.title: Three-stage pattern observed for WideResNet-28-10

nodes.content: For a ResNet-18 trained on CIFAR-10, the AUROC and FPR95 landscapes under weight perturbations along random normalized Gaussian directions $d$ with magnitude $\alpha$ ($\theta(\alpha) = \theta_{\text{final}} + \alpha \cdot d$) show that a small perturbation of $\alpha \approx 0.1$ causes AUROC to drop from approximately 94% to 88% and FPR95 to increase from approximately 32% to 50%, quantitatively demonstrating that the trained solution lies in a narrow optimum in weight space with respect to OOD metrics.

metadata.credit: This direct visualization preempts the concern that the instability is merely a statistical fluctuation or an artifact of evaluation noise. Without this landscape analysis, the claim that the model is fragile to small weight perturbations would be based only on the observation that nearby checkpoints have different AUROC, which could be due to other factors (e.g., different learning progress). The quantitative demonstration that moving weights by a small magnitude in a random direction causes large metric changes provides direct evidence for the narrow-optima mechanism, underwriting the mechanistic layer of the conclusion.

nodes.title: Direct landscape visualization shows narrow optima

nodes.content: For a ResNet-18 trained on CIFAR-10, the exponential moving average of parameters (model averaging, MA) reduces the sensitivity of AUROC and FPR95 to weight perturbations across six scoring functions: MSP, ODIN, Energy, Mahalanobis, KNN, and ViM, as shown by the flatter landscapes for the averaged model compared to the original model.

metadata.credit: This cross-scoring-function consistency preempts the concern that MA's stabilization might be specific to one scoring function (e.g., MSP) and not generalize to others. Without this evidence, the conclusion that MA stabilizes OOD metrics would be limited to the tested scoring function. The credit underwrites the generalization of the stabilization claim across different OOD detection methods.

nodes.title: MA stabilizes OOD metrics across multiple scoring functions

nodes.content: For the linear-Gaussian model where ID features are drawn from $\mathcal{N}(y \cdot \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{ID}}, \sigma^2 \boldsymbol{I})$ with $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{ID}} = (1, \eta, \dots, \eta) \in \mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ and OOD features from $\mathcal{N}(q \cdot \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{OOD}}, \sigma^2 \boldsymbol{I})$ with $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{OOD}} = (0, \eta, \dots, \eta)$, the Bayes optimal classifier $f_{\text{Bayes}}(\boldsymbol{x}) = x_1 + \eta \sum_{i=2}^{d+1} x_i$ yields closed-form ID classification risk $\mathcal{R}_{\text{ID}} = \Pr\{\mathcal{N}(0,1) > \sqrt{1 + d \eta^2} / \sigma\}$ and OOD detection risk $\mathcal{R}_{\text{OOD}} = \Pr\{\mathcal{N}(0,1) > (\delta - d \eta^2) / (\sigma \sqrt{1 + d \eta^2})\} + \Pr\{\mathcal{N}(0,1) > (\delta + d \eta^2) / (\sigma \sqrt{1 + d \eta^2})\}$, showing that increasing the number of common features $d$ increases OOD risk while only slowly decreasing ID risk.

metadata.credit: This rigorous derivation preempts the concern that the relationship between common features and OOD risk is merely conjectural. Without this formal result, the claim that abundant common features harm OOD detection would be based only on intuition. The derivation provides a precise mathematical expression showing that OOD risk increases with $d$ (through the term $d \eta^2$ in the numerator of the Gaussian tail probability), underwriting the quantitative layer of the conclusion and providing a concrete target for intervention (reducing effective $d$).

nodes.title: Closed-form derivation of ID and OOD risks for Bayes classifier

nodes.content: For the linear-Gaussian model with squared-error empirical risk and LASSO regularization parameter $\lambda$, the minimizer is $f_{\text{LASSO}}(\boldsymbol{x}) = (1 - \lambda)_+ \cdot x_1 + \sum_{i=2}^{d+1} (\eta - \lambda)_+ \cdot x_i$, where $(\cdot)_+$ denotes the positive part. This closed-form solution shows that the $L_1$ penalty sets coefficients to zero for common features where $\eta < \lambda$, thereby reducing the effective number of common features and decreasing OOD risk at controlled cost to ID risk.

metadata.credit: This analytic solution preempts the concern that sparsity-inducing regularization might not selectively target common features. Without this result, the connection between pruning and OOD detection would be purely heuristic. The derivation shows that LASSO sets coefficients to zero for features where $\eta < \lambda$, providing a principled mechanism for feature selection that reduces OOD risk at controlled cost to ID accuracy. This underwrites the mechanistic layer of the conclusion, showing how sparsity can reduce the effective number of common features.

nodes.title: Closed-form LASSO solution shows feature selection mechanism

nodes.content: The Average of Pruning (AoP) pipeline is specified with explicit pseudocode (Algorithm 1) for iterative magnitude pruning with weight rewind (20% pruning per iteration, rewind to initial training step $k$) and an explicit formula for the exponential moving average of parameters: $\theta_{t+1}^{\text{MA}} = \theta_t$ for $t < t_0$, and $\theta_{t+1}^{\text{MA}} = \tau \cdot \theta_t^{\text{MA}} + (1 - \tau) \cdot \theta_{t+1}$ for $t \ge t_0$ with $\tau = (t - t_0) / (t - t_0 + 1)$, enabling reproducible implementation.

metadata.credit: This detailed specification preempts the concern that AoP is an ill-defined or irreproducible method. Without the pseudocode and explicit formulas, practitioners would not be able to implement the method reliably. The clear description underwrites the computational reproducibility of the conclusion, ensuring that the reported empirical results can be independently verified.

nodes.title: Clear specification of AoP pipeline with pseudocode and formulas

nodes.content: AoP is evaluated as a plug-in module on top of six post-hoc OOD scoring functions (MSP, ODIN, Energy, KNN, ViM, MaxLogit) and in combination with Outlier Exposure (OE), showing consistent AUROC and FPR95 improvements across all scoring functions on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 benchmarks.

metadata.credit: This compatibility evidence preempts the concern that AoP might only work with specific scoring functions or require modifications to the scoring pipeline. Without this evidence, the claim that AoP is a "simple module readily pluggable into any existing method" would be unsupported. The credit underwrites the generalization of AoP across different OOD detection approaches.

nodes.title: AoP compatible with multiple scoring functions and OE

nodes.content: AoP is evaluated on four in-distribution datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet), five architectures (ResNet-18, WideResNet-28-10, VGG-16, WideResNet-40-2, MobileNet), and multiple scoring functions (MSP, ODIN, Energy, KNN, ViM, MaxLogit, Mahalanobis, GradNorm, ReAct, VOS), with consistent AUROC and FPR95 improvements across the vast majority of settings.

metadata.credit: This breadth of evaluation preempts the concern that AoP's improvements might be specific to a particular dataset, architecture, or scoring function. Without this comprehensive evaluation, the conclusion that AoP is a generally effective plug-in module would be vulnerable to the criticism that it only works in narrow settings. The credit underwrites the generalization of AoP's efficacy across the OOD detection landscape.

nodes.title: Comprehensive evaluation across datasets, architectures, and scoring functions

nodes.content: On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, AoP applied to KNN reduces average FPR95 across six OOD datasets from 34.42% to 25.30% (a 9.1 percentage-point decrease); on CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18, AoP applied to KNN reduces FPR95 from 69.72% to 58.01% (an 11.7 point decrease); on CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18, AoP applied to ViM reduces FPR95 from 72.90% to 59.28% (a 13.6 point decrease). These reductions are large relative to the reported standard deviations (e.g., 1.63 points for CIFAR-10 KNN FPR95).

metadata.credit: These large FPR95 reductions preempt the concern that AoP's improvements are marginal or practically insignificant. Without these large effect sizes, the conclusion that AoP substantially improves OOD detection would be weaker. The credit underwrites the practical significance of AoP, showing that it can meaningfully reduce the false positive rate for OOD detection.

nodes.title: Large FPR95 reductions on CIFAR benchmarks

nodes.content: For ResNet-18 trained on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, and for WideResNet-28-10 trained on CIFAR-10, the AUROC based on MSP as a function of global sparsity (from 0% to approximately 95%) shows a non-monotone relationship: AUROC first increases from the dense baseline as sparsity increases to around 60-80%, then decreases as sparsity exceeds approximately 90%, with the optimal sparsity varying by dataset and architecture.

metadata.credit: This systematic sweep of sparsity levels preempts the concern that the improvement from pruning is coincidental or specific to a single sparsity level. Without this sweep, the conclusion that pruning helps OOD detection would be based on a single sparsity point. The non-monotone pattern provides evidence that pruning removes harmful common features before removing useful discriminative features, underwriting the mechanistic layer of the conclusion.

nodes.title: Systematic sparsity sweep shows non-monotone AUROC relationship

nodes.content: On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, three iterative pruning strategies are compared at sparsity levels 60%, 80%, and 90%: LTH with weight rewind achieves the highest AUROC (e.g., 93.14% at 60% sparsity), outperforming random pruning and fine-tuning-based pruning. Additionally, three during-training pruning methods (GMP, RigL, GraNet) all achieve AUROC above the dense baseline (91.63%) at 60-90% sparsity, though lower than LTH.

metadata.credit: This comprehensive comparison preempts the concern that the OOD improvement is specific to LTH and not a general property of pruning. Without this comparison, the conclusion that pruning reduces OOD overfitting would be limited to one pruning method. The credit underwrites the generalization of the pruning benefit across different pruning algorithms, while also identifying LTH as the most effective for OOD tasks.

nodes.title: Comparison of multiple pruning methods shows LTH is best but others also help

nodes.content: On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18 and MSP scoring, the baseline AUROC is 91.63%; with pruning only (LTH, approximately 86% sparsity) AUROC increases to 92.94%; with pruning plus model averaging (AoP) AUROC further increases to 93.32%. For WideResNet-28-10, baseline AUROC is 91.24%; pruning only gives 93.43%; AoP gives 93.99%. Similar trends hold for AUPR and FPR95 metrics.

metadata.credit: This controlled comparison preempts the concern that the improvements from AoP might be due to either component alone. Without this ablation, the conclusion that both components contribute would be based on indirect evidence. The credit underwrites the claim that pruning and MA have complementary roles, with pruning reducing overfitting and MA stabilizing the landscape.

nodes.title: Ablation shows both pruning and MA contribute to AoP gains

nodes.content: On CIFAR-10 with WideResNet-40-2, AoP applied to MSP improves misclassification detection AUROC from 92.51% to 93.23%, reduces AURC from $7.55 \times 10^{-3}$ to $6.41 \times 10^{-3}$, and reduces FPR95 from 40.87% to 38.47%. On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, AoP improves MSP AUROC from 93.41% to 93.77%. On CIFAR-100 with VGG-16, AoP improves MSP AUROC from 85.91% to 86.51%. Consistent improvements are observed across architectures and datasets.

metadata.credit: This multi-architecture, multi-metric consistency preempts the concern that the misclassification detection improvement is specific to one architecture or metric. Without this breadth, the conclusion would be vulnerable to the criticism that AoP only helps for a particular model or evaluation metric. The credit underwrites the generalization of AoP's benefit to misclassification detection across different settings.

nodes.title: Consistent misclassification detection improvements across architectures and metrics

steps.reasoning: Define the out-of-distribution (OOD) detection task used by the authors: a detector is a scalar scoring function $\phi(x)$ that maps an input image $x$ to a scalar; given a threshold $\delta$ a sample is declared OOD if $\phi(x)>\delta$ and in-distribution (ID) otherwise; area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUROC) is used as a primary, threshold-independent measure of OOD detection performance, where AUROC is the area under the curve of True Positive Rate versus False Positive Rate as the threshold varies.

Observe the authors' empirical setup for tracking training dynamics: models are trained with standard supervised training schedules (e.g., ResNet-18 trained on CIFAR-10 for 200 epochs with learning rate drops at epochs 100 and 150), and OOD metrics (AUROC and related metrics such as AUPR and FPR95) are evaluated repeatedly along the optimization trajectory to produce curves of OOD performance versus epoch; these repeated evaluations are the basis for the empirical characterization in the conclusion.
Fig. 1(a)

Report the three distinct stages of OOD detection performance observed in the AUROC curve during training (as conceptualized by the authors): (A) an initial learning stage in which both training error and test (ID) error decrease and AUROC increases; (B) a subsequent overfitting stage in which the training error approaches zero while test (ID) error can still decrease but AUROC decreases (the authors describe this as OOD overfitting caused by memorization and learning of redundant common features); and (C) a final instability stage in which classification test error is relatively stable while AUROC and other OOD metrics vary sharply across nearby checkpoints, implying that selecting the final checkpoint is unreliable for OOD performance.
Fig. 1(a)

Provide empirical evidence for stage (B), the overfitting stage: the authors train architectures with varying capacity (WideResNet widths) and show that as width increases the test (ID) accuracy increases steadily while AUROC first increases and then decreases; this indicates a regime where continuing to increase model capacity or to train past zero training error causes degradation in OOD detection while ID classification performance can continue improving, which the authors interpret as overfitting in the sense of learning abundant weak common features that increase ID/OOD overlap.
Fig. 3(a)

Provide empirical evidence for stage (C), the instability stage: the authors visualize AUROC (and related metrics) across final-stage optimization checkpoints and show that AUROC can vary sharply from one nearby checkpoint to another while the classification (ID) test error remains stable; this sharp variation demonstrates that the final-checkpoint choice is unreliable for OOD performance because a nearby checkpoint may achieve substantially different AUROC.
Fig. 1(c)

Support generality of the three-stage phenomenon across metrics, datasets and architectures: the authors report that instability and overfitting occur for multiple OOD metrics (AUROC, AUPR, FPR95) and across several OOD datasets (Textures, SVHN, LSUN-Crop, LSUN-Resize, Place365, iSUN) and across multiple networks (ResNet-18, WideResNet variants); the authors show AUROC curves and also AUPR and FPR95 curves during training that display the same stage decomposition and instability behavior.
Fig. 12
Fig. 13

Summarize the practical consequence emphasized by the authors: because (B) overfitting degrades OOD detection even while ID error improves, and (C) instability produces sharp variations in OOD metrics near the end of training, practitioners cannot reliably use the final training checkpoint for OOD detection without additional remedies; this motivates the authors' subsequent investigation and method proposals.

Treat conclusion 1 (the empirical three-stage dynamics and late-stage instability of OOD metrics) as established knowledge for this derivation; the instability stage means AUROC can vary sharply between nearby checkpoints while classification error is stable.

Formulate the weight-perturbation experiment the authors use to analyze instability: denote the final trained parameter vector by $\theta_{\text{final}}$, draw a random direction $d$ (the authors draw $d$ from a Gaussian distribution and normalize it following the procedure in the cited loss-landscape visualization work), and consider perturbed weights
$$
\theta(d,\alpha)=\theta_{\text{final}}+\alpha\cdot d,
$$
where $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ is a scalar magnitude parameter; the authors evaluate OOD metrics (AUROC and FPR95) as functions of $\alpha$ for multiple random directions $d$ to visualize metric landscapes around the solution.
Fig. 2(c)
[30]

Report the empirical finding from the landscape: the AUROC and FPR95 landscapes under small $\alpha$ show narrow optima around $\alpha=0$, i.e., the trained solution is fragile so that small perturbations of the network weights produce sharp metric changes; the authors summarize this as the presence of narrow optima (fragility) for OOD metrics in weight space, which explains the observed checkpoint-to-checkpoint instability in AUROC during the final training stage.
Fig. 2(c)

Connect MA to landscape widening and empirical stabilization: the authors invoke prior interpretations that weight averaging (e.g., stochastic weight averaging) approximates an ensemble and yields a flatter/wider optimum; empirically, the averaged parameters $\theta^{\mathrm{MA}}$ produce smoother AUROC curves during training and reduced sensitivity of AUROC and FPR95 to small weight perturbations compared to the unaveraged final checkpoint, as shown by comparing the metric landscapes and training-time AUROC curves for original versus averaged models.
Fig. 2(b)
Fig. 2(d)

Note implementation details used by the authors in experiments to realize MA: the authors set the MA start epoch $t_0$ to 100 in CIFAR training experiments and use the specified decay formula for $\tau$; MA is applied with negligible extra computational cost compared to full ensembles and thus is a practical stabilization method.

State the simplified probabilistic data model used by the authors to derive closed-form risks: input feature vectors $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$, labels $y$ for ID data and $q$ for OOD data are drawn uniformly from $\{-1,+1\}$ (notation $y\stackrel{u.a.r.}{\sim}\{-1,+1\}$, $q\stackrel{u.a.r.}{\sim}\{-1,+1\}$); ID features are Gaussian with mean $y\cdot\boldsymbol{\mu}_\text{ID}$ and isotropic variance $\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I}$, OOD features are Gaussian with mean $q\cdot\boldsymbol{\mu}_\text{OOD}$ and the same isotropic variance; explicitly,
$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_\text{ID}=(1,\eta,\dots,\eta),\qquad \boldsymbol{\mu}_\text{OOD}=(0,\eta,\dots,\eta),
$$
with $0<\eta\ll1$ representing weak common features and $d\gg1$ representing many such features.

Define the Bayes optimal linear logit under the ID distribution given the preceding model assumptions: the Bayes logit (scalar output before sign) is
$$
f_{\mathrm{Bayes}}(\boldsymbol{x}) = x_1 + \eta\sum_{i=2}^{d+1} x_i,
$$
where $x_1$ is the special discriminative feature (different between ID and OOD) and $x_2,\dots,x_{d+1}$ are common features shared between ID and OOD.

Define the two risk quantities the authors analyze: (i) the in-distribution classification risk $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{ID}}(f)$ defined as the probability that $\operatorname{sign}(f(\boldsymbol{x}))\neq y$ when $(\boldsymbol{x},y)\sim\mathcal{D}_\text{ID}$; and (ii) the OOD rejection risk $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{OOD}}(f)$ defined as the probability that $|f(\boldsymbol{x})|>\delta$ when $(\boldsymbol{x},q)\sim\mathcal{D}_\text{OOD}$, where $\delta$ is a chosen rejection threshold.

Derive closed-form expressions for the risks of the Bayes classifier under the Gaussian assumptions (the derivation is provided in the paper's supplementary proofs): the in-distribution classification risk simplifies to
$$
\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{ID}}(f_{\mathrm{Bayes}})=\Pr\!\left\{\mathcal{N}(0,1)>\frac{\sqrt{1+d\eta^2}}{\sigma}\right\},
$$
and the OOD rejection risk simplifies to
$$
\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{OOD}}(f_{\mathrm{Bayes}})=\Pr\!\left\{\mathcal{N}(0,1)>\frac{\delta-d\eta^2}{\sigma\sqrt{1+d\eta^2}}\right\}+\Pr\!\left\{\mathcal{N}(0,1)>\frac{\delta+d\eta^2}{\sigma\sqrt{1+d\eta^2}}\right\},
$$
where $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ denotes a standard normal random variable; these formulas follow from computing the mean and variance of the Gaussian linear combination $x_1+\eta\sum_{i=2}^{d+1} x_i$ under the specified ID and OOD distributions and converting to standard-normal tail probabilities.
Fig. 4(a)

Interpret the risk formulas to link common-feature abundance to OOD risk: for fixed small $\eta>0$ and large $d$, the term $d\eta^2$ grows with the number $d$ of weak common features, which increases the numerator terms in the OOD risk expressions and therefore increases $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{OOD}}$ markedly, while the in-distribution classification risk $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{ID}}$ depends on $\sqrt{1+d\eta^2}$ and thus improves only slowly; the authors illustrate this behavior numerically for $\sigma=1,\eta=0.01$ in a plot showing $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{ID}}$ decreasing slowly and $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{OOD}}$ increasing sharply as $d$ increases.
Fig. 4(a)

Introduce a squared-error empirical risk with an $L_1$ penalty (LASSO) as a feature-selection analogue in the linear model and state the optimization objective:
$$
\min_{\boldsymbol{w}}\ \mathbb{E}_{(\boldsymbol{x},y)\sim\mathcal{D}_\text{ID}}\!\left\{\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\boldsymbol{w}^\top\boldsymbol{x}}{\sigma}-y\right)^2+\lambda\|\boldsymbol{w}\|_1\right\},
$$
where $\lambda\ge0$ is the $L_1$ regularization parameter; the expectation is over the ID distribution previously defined.

State the closed-form LASSO solution for this simplified model derived in the paper: the trimmed coefficient vector is
$$
f_{\text{LASSO}}(\boldsymbol{x}) = (1-\lambda)_+\,x_1 + \sum_{i=2}^{d+1} (\eta-\lambda)_+\, x_i,
$$
where $(\cdot)_+$ denotes the positive part (i.e., $(u)_+=\max\{0,u\}$); the derivation uses that the covariance $\mathbb{E}[xx^\top]/\sigma^2$ is the identity under the model and that $\mathbb{E}[xy]/\sigma$ equals $(1,\eta,\dots,\eta)^\top$, giving the stated soft-threshold solution.

Explain how the LASSO solution connects to reducing OOD risk: choosing $\lambda\approx\eta$ zeroes out or greatly reduces the coefficients on the abundant weak common features (because $(\eta-\lambda)_+\approx0$), thereby reducing $d\eta^2$ and substantially lowering $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{OOD}}$ at only a controlled increase in $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{ID}}$; the authors illustrate this trade-off numerically in a plot of $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{ID}}$ and $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{OOD}}$ versus $\lambda$.

State as known the upstream results used in this derivation: conclusion 2 (model averaging stabilizes OOD metrics by widening optima) and conclusion 6 (pruning reduces OOD overfitting by eliminating abundant weak common features) are treated as established starting points; AoP combines these two components to address instability and overfitting simultaneously.

Provide the high-level description of AoP (Average of Pruning) as the pipeline that combines pruning and model averaging to mitigate OOD overfitting and instability, and emphasize the design goal: AoP is intended as a practical, architecture-agnostic, drop-in module that can be applied to any post-hoc OOD scoring method without modifying the scoring function.

Describe Step 1 of AoP: iterative magnitude pruning with weight rewinding (Lottery Ticket / IMP with rewind protocol) in operational detail as the authors implement it: initialize binary mask $m=1^n$, train the network from initial parameters $\theta_0$ to a rewind checkpoint $\theta_k$, then for each pruning iteration train the masked network $m\odot\theta_k$ to $m\odot\theta_T$, prune the globally lowest-magnitude 20% of weights to update mask $m$, rewind weights back to $\theta_k$, and repeat $N$ times; in the CIFAR experiments the authors prune 20% per iteration and perform 9 iterations to reach approximately 86% sparsity.

Describe Step 2 of AoP: apply exponential moving-weight averaging (MA) either during or after pruning using the authors' MA update:
$$
\theta_{t+1}^{\mathrm{MA}}=\begin{cases}
\theta_t, & t<t_0,\\[4pt]
\tau\cdot \theta_t^{\mathrm{MA}} + (1-\tau)\cdot \theta_{t+1}, & t\ge t_0,
\end{cases}
$$
with the implementation choice $t_0=100$ epochs in CIFAR training and decay $\tau=\dfrac{t-t_0}{t-t_0+1}$; the averaged parameters $\theta^{\mathrm{MA}}$ are maintained throughout training so that the final averaged, pruned parameter vector is available.

Describe Step 3 of AoP: form the final model by applying the learned binary mask to the averaged parameters and use the resulting pruned-and-averaged model $f(x;\,m\odot\theta^{\mathrm{MA}})$ as a drop-in replacement for the original model when computing any post-hoc OOD scoring function (examples include MSP, ODIN, Energy, ViM, KNN, MaxLogit, etc.); no change to the scoring rules themselves is required.

Explain the conceptual roles of the two components and why they are combined: pruning (Step 1) reduces the model's tendency to memorize and to learn abundant weak common features (addressing the overfitting phenomenon identified and theoretically motivated via LASSO), while model averaging (Step 2) produces a wider, smoother optimum in weight space that stabilizes OOD metrics against small perturbations (addressing the instability phenomenon); combining both components yields a model that both avoids OOD overfitting and yields stable OOD metrics at deployment time.

Note practical implementation details and low-barrier nature emphasized by the authors: AoP requires only standard pruning (IMP) infrastructure and a running exponential moving average of weights (negligible extra compute), and the final pruned-averaged model integrates readily with existing OOD pipelines without retraining scoring procedures.

open_questions.content: The paper acknowledges several scientifically meaningful unresolved issues and limitations left for future work: (1) theoretical generalization gap — the formal analysis linking sparsity to reduced OOD risk is derived in a linear Gaussian toy model (LASSO solution); extending a rigorous theoretical justification of why and when pruning reduces OOD risk for nonlinear deep networks remains unresolved (the paper notes "LASSO is not suitable for neural networks" and uses pruning heuristically motivated by the linear analysis); (2) pruning algorithm efficiency and optimality — the primary pruning method used is iterative magnitude pruning with weight rewinding (LTH), which is computationally intensive; although several during-training pruning methods (GMP, RigL, GraNet) were evaluated and shown to help, they yielded weaker OOD gains than LTH in these experiments; designing more efficient pruning schedules or training-time sparse training algorithms that match LTH's OOD benefits is unresolved; (3) formal guarantees for AUROC stability under model averaging — model averaging empirically stabilizes OOD metrics and approximates ensembling, but a formal understanding of how averaging parameters affects OOD scoring functions (beyond empirical landscape visualizations) is not provided; (4) hyperparameter selection and transferability — choices such as pruning fraction per iteration, rewind step $k$, number of pruning iterations, starting epoch $t_0$ for averaging, and the decay $\tau$ were set empirically (e.g. 20% per iteration, $t_0=100$ on CIFAR) and their principled selection across architectures, dataset scales, and different scanning of near- vs far-OOD regimes remains an open practical question. These limitations are explicitly acknowledged in the manuscript and motivate further theoretical and algorithmic work.
